definition: Prurient means showing an excessive, unwholesome interest in indecent matters.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word prurient. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know prurient should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The landlady called her window-watching neighborly concern, but the notebook logging every tenant's visitors suggested something more prurient.
Curious is far milder than prurient — an open, healthy wanting-to-know.
Nosy stops short of prurient: the nosy neighbor pries into any business at all, while prurient interest fixes, unwholesomely, on the indecent kind.

Voyeuristic means peeping at private moments for the thrill of watching unseen. Prurient judges the appetite rather than the method: an excessive, unwholesome interest in the indecent, whatever alibi it wears. A voyeur has to hide to look; a prurient reader can flip magazine pages in broad daylight.

Leering is the look itself — openly eyeing what decency says to look away from, right there on the face. Prurient names the appetite behind such looks: an unwholesome interest in the indecent that can wear a respectable excuse. A leer is visible; prurient interest can pass for concern.

Latin prurire, 'to itch,' left almost nothing else in everyday English — its only other descendant, the medical term pruritus, stays inside dermatology clinics. The itch survives in prurient alone.
Prurient means showing an excessive, unwholesome interest in indecent matters.
The gallery billed its exhibition as a study of censorship; the visitors who skipped every wall text and crowded straight to the banned photographs made the show's real, prurient appeal hard to deny.
Prurient condemns the appetite, not the material: it describes the itch to peer at indecent things under whatever respectable excuse is handy.
Curiosity can be healthy and nosiness merely rude; prurient interest has crossed into the unwholesome.
Prurient always accuses — it says the interest itself is dirty, whatever alibi it wears.
Pair it with interest, curiosity, or appeal.
Its unit neighbors carve up the territory: profane is offensive language or irreverence, ribald is crude humor, and prurient is the audience's unwholesome itch to look.

When the state senator's divorce filing leaked, the Gazette's inbox filled overnight with tips, photographs, and offers to sell more.
The editor printed the filing's public facts in four paragraphs and declined the rest.
One ran a week of stories the editor described as prurient — reporting in name only, feeding an unwholesome itch for the couple's private wreckage under the banner of accountability.
'There is a difference,' she wrote in a column, 'between what the public needs to know and what some of the public would enjoy knowing.' Circulation dipped for a month.
Then the trial ended, the rivals moved on, and the Gazette's subscribers, notably, stayed.
